content: 1. Network-based approaches can be implemented as a method for HIV testing among key populations, integrated into a comprehensive care and prevention package. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. 2. HIV self-testing should be offered as an HIV testing strategy. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 3. In all settings, HIV testing services (HTS) with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care are recommended for adolescents from key populations. This is a strong recommendation, though based on very low-quality evidence. 4. In high HIV burden settings, HTS should be provided to all adolescents, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care. This is a strong recommendation, but the evidence quality is very low. 5. In low HIV burden settings, the World Health Organization (WHO) suggests that HTS with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care should be accessible to all adolescents. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 6. In all settings, adolescents should be counseled about the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV-positive status. They should be empowered and supported to decide if, when, how, and to whom they disclose their status. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 7. Provider-assisted referral should be offered to people with HIV as part of a voluntary, comprehensive package of testing and care. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 8. Governments should review age-of-consent policies to ensure that adolescents’ rights to make decisions about their health and well-being are upheld. This should take into account varying levels of maturity and understanding. 9. HIV and syphilis testing during early pregnancy allows pregnant women to access prevention, treatment, and care services, reducing the risk of transmission to their infants and sexual partners. 10. Early treatment for HIV and syphilis, combined with prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) interventions (e.g., antivirals and infant HBV vaccination), and identifying women needing long-term treatment for chronic HBV, results in optimal health outcomes for mothers and children. 11. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is most effective in preventing HIV transmission from mothers to infants when initiated before or early in pregnancy. 12. These services can be delivered at antenatal care (ANC) clinics or through safe abortion services where legally permitted. 13. Linkage to the full package of reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health (RMNCH) services is essential for all women and HIV-exposed infants, regardless of their HIV status. 14. All RMNCH and ANC services should offer HTS, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) testing at least once, ideally during the first trimester or as early as possible in pregnancy. This is particularly important in settings with an HBsAg prevalence of ≥2% in the general population. 15. Women who test positive should be promptly linked to care, treatment, and prevention services. 16. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can be used as the first test in antenatal care settings and may be cost-saving in all settings. 17. Maternal HIV retesting during pregnancy and breastfeeding is recommended for all women in high HIV burden settings. Women should be counseled about the risks of HIV acquisition, the benefits of retesting, the retesting schedule, and the importance of bringing their children to services during the first year of life. 18. In low HIV burden settings, maternal retesting in the third trimester is recommended only for women at high ongoing HIV risk, such as those from key populations or with partners who are HIV-positive but not on ART or virally suppressed. 19. Offering retesting to all pregnant women in low HIV burden settings is not cost-effective unless part of efforts to achieve elimination of mother-to-child transmission (eMTCT). 20. Postpartum maternal retesting may be delivered alongside infant immunization services. 21. Pregnant women already diagnosed with HIV and on ART, or those treated for syphilis during their current pregnancy, should not be tested with a dual HIV/syphilis RDT. Instead, they should be tested for HIV and syphilis using separate tests according to national algorithms. 22. Pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should start ART immediately or as soon as possible after an HIV-positive diagnosis, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count, and continue treatment for life. 23. Pregnant women who are HIV-negative but at ongoing risk should be linked to comprehensive HIV prevention services. 24. It is safe for pregnant and breastfeeding women to start or continue taking pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). 25. Pregnant and breastfeeding women taking PrEP should receive HIV testing and STI testing at quarterly facility visits. 26. HTS can serve as an entry point for a range of pregnancy care and prevention services, including screening and treatment for other infections (e.g., STIs, hepatitis, and TB), HIV prevention, and sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception and family planning. 27. The presence of STIs increases the risk of HIV acquisition. 28. All HIV-exposed infants should receive HIV testing to determine their status and start ART immediately if HIV-positive. 29. Virological testing, such as nucleic acid testing (NAT), is required for infants under 18 months of age due to the persistence of maternal antibodies. After this period, serology tests, including RDTs, can be used. 30. Early infant diagnosis (EID) using NAT technologies within two months of birth has improved, but only 56% of HIV-exposed infants received EID by the second month of age in 2018. 31. Delays in obtaining test results and further losses in the treatment cascade still occur, resulting in less than one-third of perinatally infected infants being linked to services and initiating ART in a timely manner. 32. NAT at birth can be considered to improve EID coverage among HIV-exposed infants. This approach is conditionally recommended by WHO and involves NAT at birth or within two days of birth in addition to existing EID approaches. 33. Mathematical modeling suggests that in resource-limited settings, prioritizing EID at six weeks over adding NAT at birth may be more effective when uptake or retention in the testing cascade is suboptimal. 34. In all settings, HTS should be offered to all biological infants and young children with an HIV-positive parent whose HIV status is unknown, as part of a provider-assisted referral package. 35. Additional support may be required for orphans and vulnerable children in high HIV burden settings, where one or both parents may have died. 36. Lay providers delivering testing through community outreach may also play a role in improving access to HTS.
